REUTERS/Stelios Misinas AGIOS KONSTANTINOS, Greece, Aug 2 (Reuters) - Two firefighting helicopters collided in Greece while helping to control a huge wildfire on Sunday that has destroyed more than 100 homes northwest of Athens, while people fled another blaze on the tourist island of Kefalonia. Two people on one helicopter — a Greek and a Danish national — died, while the crew on the other, one person ‌from Greece, one from Britain, survived, the fire service said. Investigations had started into what caused the collision, it added. Europe has been ravaged by wildfires this summer after a period of record-breaking heatwaves ‌and little rain – conditions that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. Advertisement Advertisement Destructive blazes in France and Spain showed some signs of easing over the weekend, but several wildfires have broken out in Greece after a period of relative calm there. The two helicopters collided in the ​area of Psatha in the Attica region, Greece's fire service said in a statement. Video posted on the Forecast Weather Greece Facebook page appeared to show two helicopters closing to cross paths at low altitude, before the main rotor of the lower helicopter struck the underside of the other. The lower one then crashed in flames. The second helicopter then dumped its load of water and flew away. Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the footage. Advertisement Advertisement Investigations suggested the fire that started in the Greek region of Boeotia before spreading to Attica was caused by sparks from conductors on a private network transmitting electricity generated by wind turbines to the main power grid, the eKathimerini website reported. Two Greek nationals were ‌arrested on suspicion of negligence, while another suspect remains at large, the report ⁠said. 'FORCE OF NATURE' Gale-force winds that had fuelled a fire around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth 60 km (40 miles) northwest of Athens subsided, but flames crossed a mountain to the south and reached the settlement of Veniza and a military firing range, igniting unexploded ordnance. Advertisement Advertisement Emergency crews focused their efforts on preventing fire from advancing towards the coastal ⁠town of Megara, which has a population of around 30,000. "There are moments when the force of nature and the intensity of weather conditions exceed all human planning and every operational capability," Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in his regular Sunday message. Greek authorities issued emergency alerts for evacuations for a number of settlements in western Attica, including an industrial estate near Megara. In the village of Agios Konstantinos, residents were doing their best to halt the spread of the blaze. Advertisement Advertisement "The fire has been burning ​since ​last night, it is certain that they cannot have forces everywhere. We as residents are doing everything we can," said Tasos ​Tzempelikos, 61, who along with his son was pouring water on the fire. Overnight, several ‌settlements on the Ionian island of Kefalonia were evacuated after a fire broke out in the Pastra area in the south. FIRE IN FRANCE CHANGES COURSE In France, a fire in the southwestern Var region switched direction after a change in the wind and surged into a forested area that was difficult to access, BFM TV reported. A new fire also broke out alongside a highway near the historic southern city of Carcassonne, apparently caused by a blazing vehicle, BFM TV added. Advertisement Advertisement Video on the channel showed huge plumes of billowing grey smoke and flames near the road. Authorities said they had closed the highway and evacuated a nearby animal park. In Montfort-sur-Argens in Var, Georges Blanc, who had fled the fire earlier, returned home and was busy putting out hot embers to prevent a flare-up, while firefighters watered the wider area. "With the combined efforts of the two Canadairs (firefighting planes) and the firefighters, I think you ‌could say all the houses were saved ... And now, well, I'm coming back to check, because since I saw the flames, ​I thought the houses wouldn't have survived," he told Reuters. In central Spain, wildfires that ripped through tens of thousands of hectares over ​the past week were mostly under control, though firefighters were dealing with reignitions in some areas. Advertisement Advertisement In ​the western province of Caceres, a forest blaze erupted on Saturday, prompting the evacuation of around 800 people. Those residents were allowed to return on Sunday but remained confined to ‌their homes as the fire was still active. HUNGARY NUCLEAR PLANT FORCED TO SHUT Other ​European countries are struggling with drought and receding water levels ​in major rivers, including the Rhine and the Danube, which recorded its lowest-ever water levels in Hungary, Serbia and Romania. Hungary faces a critical five days, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, as the drying out of the Danube forced the country's sole nuclear power plant to shut for the first time in more than four decades, with a new heatwave looming. Advertisement Advertisement Falls in water levels amid a lack ​of rain have also disrupted shipping and tourism in Hungary and triggered water-use ‌restrictions in more than 100 cities and villages. Danube levels in Serbia fell to their lowest since 1985, cutting the daily output of the country's biggest hydropower plant to only 20%, the ​energy minister said on Sunday. Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Women and children walk at camp for internally displaced people in Yemen. Photograph: Reuters Yemen Children forced to give up school for work as fighting upends daily life in Yemen Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm Nasser al-Sakkaf in Taiz and William Christou Mon 28 Sep 2026 03.07 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 06.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the afternoons he helped his father feed the livestock. He took his studies seriously, dreaming of becoming the first teacher in his family of farmers. As fighting approached his village in al-Wazeyah district in Taiz, Yemen, two weeks ago, Muneer’s focus started to drift from his lessons. The classroom echoed with the distant sounds of explosions and gunfire. His home was suddenly on the frontline of renewed fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. “We heard there was fighting in surrounding areas but we didn’t expect it would reach our village that fast,” Muneer said. “As soon as the sounds of clashes approached our village, we took our livestock and important belongings and fled home early in the morning.” He and his family fled south-west, moving to a camp set up for displaced people in al-Shimayateen, Taiz. They arrived penniless and lacking even the most basic supplies. Muneer and his family are some of the more than 130,000 people displaced by recent fighting in Yemen, which started in September when the Houthis launched a renewed military campaign and rapidly moved south-west , seizing control of towns along the Red Sea coast. The Houthis’ campaign interrupted years of relative calm that had prevailed over Yemen , with frontlines remaining broadly static since a UN-mediated ceasefire came into force in 2022. The Houthis are now battling government forces and a Saudi air campaign to seize strategic highlands and supply lines on the outskirts of Taiz. Civilians have been driven out of their homes by the fighting, fleeing airstrikes and missiles. Muneer and his brother, instead of studying, now sell socks and other cheap products in the markets outside his displacement camp. His classroom has been replaced by a small tent where he and his five siblings and parents crowd together in the humid night air. He joins the more than 3.2 million children whose studies were interrupted by Yemen’s civil war prior to this month’s escalation. View image in fullscreen Displaced Yemenis carry water back to their makeshift camps. Photograph: Ebrahim Al-Suhaibi/Reuters “Studying is important, but not in a situation like this where we are struggling to get enough food, water and other necessities,” he said. “For now, I will keep working until the war ends.” His father, Ghaleb Farie, has been forced to ask his sons to work so that the family can scrape together enough to survive life in the displacement camp. Farie hopes the camp will be only a temporary home and that he can soon return to his village, but he is not optimistic as new displaced people arrive every day. “What I was told by neighbours who have been displaced for longer is that the first few months are difficult and I will adapt,” Farie said. Life has also grown harder for those who have remained in their homes. Abdulwasea Abdu, the principal of Musaab Ibn Umayr school in Taiz, tried to keep the doors of his school open for as long as possible to give children a sense of normality. But that normality was shattered two weeks ago when a missile fell nearby, exploding in sight of the students. “On the day the missile struck, we witnessed severe panic among them, with crying and screaming due to the explosions. Some children showed psychological trauma as a result of the intensity of the blasts,” Abdu said. The school was forced to close its doors, depriving the more than 600 pupils of their education. Abdu watches the battlefield developments closely, searching for a let-up that will let him resume classes, but so far the situation has been too chaotic. “The area faces fighting from multiple fronts – south, west and north – which makes it difficult to take any steps toward resuming classes at the moment,” Abdu said. He fears that many of the children out of school and displaced will be forced into child labour. View image in fullscreen Children at al-Farsi camp for internally displaced people in southern Yemen. Photograph: Mohamad Hakim/AFP/Getty Images The resumption of fighting has upended life for residents of south-west Yemen. Clashes severed the main road between the now Houthi-controlled port city of Mocha and government-controlled Taiz. The road is a vital artery for goods as it is one of the only in the area wide enough for large trucks and passenger buses. Interrupted commerce has increased the price of basic goods, compounding the crisis, particularly for displaced people. “It is civilians who bear the cost of military escalation, and it seems that we in Taiz are paying a particularly heavy price, as commodities no longer reach us easily,” said Essam Nabil, a 56-year-old carpenter in Taiz city. He added many people had begun giving up meat and resorting to cheaper foods. The fighting has disrupted other, more mundane facets of daily life. Asaad, an expatriate who works in Saudi Arabia and asked to be identified only by his first name, can no longer take a direct trip back from Yemen. “This reminds me of the early years of the war in Taiz, when the main roads were blocked and we had to travel through Aden before heading to Saudi Arabia,” Asaad said. “Now, we are repeating the same expensive and arduous journey.” Explore more on these topics Yemen Houthis Internally displaced people Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: BERLIN — Germany faces a consequential choice over building its next fighter jet: join an existing project with the U.K., Italy and Japan, or develop a new aircraft with Sweden and Spain. The decision will shape its military capabilities and diplomatic alliances for decades. The dilemma follows the collapse of the Future Combat Air System, Germany's troubled fighter project with France and Spain, leaving Berlin to reconsider how it develops advanced military technology with European partners. Defense ministry assessments favor partnering with Stockholm and Madrid, citing military requirements and opportunities for German industry, while chancellery officials , according to industry and diplomatic officials who spoke with POLITICO on the basis of anonymity to discuss sensitive issues, see diplomatic advantages in aligning with London. Advertisement Advertisement “On the one hand, all countries want to support their national industries,” Defense Minister Boris Pistorius told lawmakers in September , asked about European defense cooperation following FCAS's collapse. “At the same time, everyone ... also wants joint European armaments projects,” he said. “Resolving this dilemma is no simple matter.” Berlin's overarching goal is to become less dependent on American military technology. And while that ambition predates Washington's increasingly unpredictable approach to European security , President Donald Trump’s threats to leave NATO and criticism of allies have raised the stakes. At a campaign rally last week, the U.S. president warned that America would have “no choice but to leave” Europe — implying American troops on bases — if its leaders failed to change course on immigration. He also criticized NATO allies for refusing to support Washington’s war against Iran. Ukraine’s recent difficulties with American-controlled SpaceX satellite communications, delays in deliveries of American-made air defense missiles and problems with intelligence sharing have also highlighted how countries relying on U.S. technology can remain vulnerable to decisions made in Washington. The fighter jet decision is the most immediate test of a broader effort: Germany is also planning its own military satellite communications network that could cost €10 billion, and is working with Britain to develop European long-range missiles capable of striking targets more than 2,000 kilometers away. It also aims to meet NATO’s core defense spending target of 3.5 percent of GDP by 2029 — six years ahead of the alliance’s deadline. But spending more will not automatically make it militarily independent. Germany cannot develop every advanced weapon by itself, so it needs partners that can deliver military capabilities while giving Germany a lasting role in developing and controlling them. Advertisement Advertisement Lessons from expensive failures In June, Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron abandoned their plans to jointly develop Europe’s next-generation fighter jet . The FCAS project was supposed to be a flagship of European defense cooperation and replace Germany’s aging Eurofighters. Instead, it was derailed by years of industrial disagreements between Germany's Airbus Defence and France's Dassault. The collapse showed how partner disputes can tie up billions in taxpayer money in delays and abandoned ambitions. Now Germany’s immediate challenge is finding a replacement. Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz give a press conference in Brühl, Germany on July 17, 2026. | Ina Fassbender/AFP via Getty Images One possibility comes from Britain, which is already developing a next-generation aircraft with Italy and Japan under the Global Combat Air Programme, or GCAP. During a visit to Berlin earlier this month, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham offered Germany the opportunity to join . For London, German participation could help share the enormous costs of developing one of the world’s most advanced military aircraft. For Berlin, joining an existing program could offer a path forward without having to establish an entirely new project. But the proposal has met with reservations within Germany’s defense ministry. As POLITICO previously reported , internal ministry assessments recommend pursuing a new fighter program with Sweden and Spain instead. Advertisement Advertisement German officials fear joining GCAP would leave domestic industry with little say over key technologies and production, since responsibilities are already divided among the existing partners. Defense ministry officials see advantages in the Swedish option, including more compatible military requirements and greater opportunities for German industry. But that may not necessarily align with Berlin's broader diplomatic ambitions. Two political approaches Germany and Britain have been strengthening their relationship after Brexit, including with a new friendship treaty focused in part on security and defense, and cooperation on long-range missiles. A jet partnership would deepen those ties further, tying the two countries together in one of Europe’s most strategically significant defense projects. According to an official familiar with Airbus’ thinking, granted anonymity to speak freely on sensitive issues, officials in the chancellery appear drawn to GCAP partly because of those geopolitical advantages. For Berlin’s political leadership, closer defense ties with Britain could help keep a major European military power and key NATO ally closely involved in the continent’s security as Europe is pushed to assume greater responsibility for its own defense. That leaves Germany weighing the potential diplomatic gains of partnering with Britain against the military and industrial priorities officials see in a project with Sweden. Advertisement Advertisement Diplomacy ahead The political calculations could become more pressing in the coming weeks. Merz is scheduled to visit Japan on Wednesday, offering an opportunity to discuss Germany's possible involvement in GCAP with one of the program's founding members. Japan's agreement would be essential to any German entry, while Tokyo is particularly concerned about preserving the 2035 deadline, as its aging F-2 fighter jets are due to begin retiring around then. During Burnham’s visit, he and Merz agreed to task their defense teams with examining the prospect of German participation. Industry and diplomatic officials expect Merz to raise the issue during his visit to Japan. For Merz and Pistorius, the challenge is to choose partners who can help Germany build up its defense capabilities while advancing its political, military and industrial interests.
